title: Is your U.S. licence also a franchise?
description: A brand licence can also be a franchise when the complete operating arrangement meets the federal test.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: What the federal rule examines
paragraphs: The Federal Trade Commission’s Franchise Rule examines a continuing commercial relationship with three elements: association with a trademark or other commercial symbol; significant control over, or assistance with, the operator’s method of doing business; and a required payment or commitment.

A licence grants permission to use specified rights. If you also supply the operating system, the arrangement may raise franchise duties. Calling the operator an investor, distributor or licensee does not change the actual rights, support and payments.

sections.heading: Why separate purchases can form one system
paragraphs: In a fictional maintenance offer, the operator receives branded vans, mandatory scheduling software, initial training and required inspection methods, and pays a licence fee. These features work together to shape how the service is run.

The important questions are what the training teaches, what the software controls, how much discretion the operator retains and which payments are unavoidable. Software alone does not decide the test. Three separate invoices for the licence, training and software do not remove the need to consider the complete arrangement.

sections.heading: An exemption is a separate question
paragraphs: Once the arrangement is described accurately, examine any federal exclusion or exemption and its conditions. An exemption from specified duties does not necessarily change the relationship’s definition. Include promises made in presentations and ordinary practice, not just the signed contract, and payments to related companies.
State definitions and sales requirements are independent. A federal conclusion does not settle the states connected with the seller, buyer, offer or proposed outlet.

practicalOutput: Before offering the arrangement, compare the contract, actual support promises and all required payments as one business model.
limitations: This is the federal starting point; it does not classify your arrangement or establish an exemption. State and local requirements remain separate.
learningSummary: Calling the contract a licence does not decide which rules apply. A brand, a way to run the business and required payments must be examined together.
seoTitle: Franchise vs licensing: the U.S. federal test

title: When does your support shape the operator’s whole business?
description: The practical reach and importance of support matter more than the name or length of a manual.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Look at the overall operating method
paragraphs: The question is not whether you provide any help. Consider its content, significance and the operator’s reasonable reliance on it in running the business. Contractual rights to impose controls matter as well as intervention already exercised. Include pre-contract promises and routine support.
The FTC’s May 2008 explanatory guide discusses training, accounting systems, management advice and detailed manuals. It is context to read with the current rule, not a current threshold sheet.

sections.heading: A short appendix can carry substantial operating rules
paragraphs: A fictional facilities brand has a logo guide covering colours and approved name use. Its quality appendix also determines accepted accounts, staffing, sales scripts, mandatory software, service reports and remedial visits.

The second document can shape the operating business even though it is called an appendix. A requirement solely protecting legal ownership of a mark differs from broader operating instructions. But neither a logo guide nor one software subscription decides the complete test, and counting features is not a substitute for assessing the relationship.

practicalOutput: Examine what your mandatory systems and promised help actually determine before treating them as incidental to a licence.
limitations: This explains one federal element, not complete franchise status or an exemption. Current law and independent state tests remain relevant.
learningSummary: A new operator may depend on your systems to price work, allocate staff and find customers. That helps explain the federal inquiry into significant operating control or assistance.
seoTitle: Significant franchise control or assistance: what matters

title: Which payments count toward the $735 federal exemption?
description: The relevant total is not just the first invoice, and exactly $735 does not pass a less-than test.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Use the amount, period and recipients together
paragraphs: Under the stated federal exemption, aggregate required payments or commitments to the franchisor or an affiliate from before operations begin through six months after they commence. The total must be less than $735; exactly $735 is not less. Older material quoting $500 does not give the current amount for this exemption.
Required means the rule’s actual definition, including contractual or practically necessary payments and its exclusions. A commitment can matter before cash is collected.

sections.heading: Fictional example: $300 is not the whole price
paragraphs: A brand requires a $300 initial fee, $250 training payment and $250 software commitment to its affiliate within the relevant period. Assuming all three are required payments under the rule, $300 + $250 + $250 = $800. The amount condition is not met on those assumptions.
Collecting the software money later does not establish that the obligation was undertaken later. Check the commitment as well as the payment date; an unknown required amount is not zero.

sections.heading: The inventory exclusion is specific
paragraphs: The payment definition excludes reasonable quantities of inventory bought at bona fide wholesale prices for resale or lease. It does not exclude every supply purchase. Equipment or materials consumed in providing a service are not automatically inventory for resale.
This is an exemption from specified federal disclosure duties, not the franchise definition or an exemption from state franchise, business-opportunity, dealer, advertising or relationship law.

practicalOutput: Count required commitments, their recipients and timing before relying on the low-payment exemption.
limitations: The page establishes no actual exemption or approved payment structure; the full definition and transaction facts still matter.
learningSummary: The exemption requires the relevant required payments or commitments to total less than $735. Count the whole arrangement, including covered affiliate payments and the specified period.
seoTitle: The $735 franchise exemption: required payments and commitments

title: One licence per state is still several licensees
description: The narrow federal guidance is not one free franchise in every state.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Three exclusive state agreements do not become one
paragraphs: A fictional European brand proposes a Texas licence to Company A, a California licence to Company B and an Illinois licence to Company C. Each calls its local company the sole licensee. The overall plan still has three proposed licensees.

Conversely, one licensee may run several outlets. That distinction does not itself establish eligibility. Existing grants and intended later grants belong in the same analysis, not just the first signed contract.

sections.heading: What the historical material supports
paragraphs: The May 2008 FTC Compliance Guide describes a narrow single-trademark-license exclusion. Staff opinion 05-1 of January 5, 2005, concerning a particular salon arrangement under an earlier rule citation, distinguished licensees from outlets and noted that intended future licences would change the analysis.
The staff view was expressly nonbinding on the Commission. Similarity to that salon or starting with one contract does not give your plan a ruling. Independent state rules also remain.

practicalOutput: Count current and planned legal licensees separately from their outlets before relying on single-license shorthand.
limitations: This explains the narrow distinction; it decides no actual eligibility, future-grant effect or comparable state treatment.
learningSummary: Count the actual recipients of the trademark rights across the whole plan. A licensee is a person or business; an outlet is a location that licensee operates.
seoTitle: Single trademark licensee versus outlets and state licences

title: Why the outlet address is not the whole sales-law question
description: The buyer and the sales communications can connect a transaction with places beyond the proposed operation.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The buyer can live in a different state
paragraphs: In a fictional sale, a Singapore parent speaks with a New York resident about a Florida operation. A U.S. subsidiary will sell the rights and a broker introduces the parties. Florida outlet does not describe the whole transaction.

Identify the actual seller, the buyer’s residence, the operating location and where relevant communications originate or are received. The applicable state provisions determine which connections matter; this example makes no New York or Florida filing finding.

sections.heading: The sales activity happens before opening
paragraphs: Website advertising, broker introductions, meetings, territory discussions, disclosure, deposits and signing can raise different questions. Their content and any money or binding promise matter, not just a future opening date. This is not a universal prohibition on introductory calls.

Coverage, registration, notice, exemption, disclosure, advertising and ongoing relationship rules are separate questions. An unresearched answer is not no requirement, and an operating permit is not sales authority.

sections.heading: A federal process does not replace the state rules
paragraphs: The federal rule preserves state and local franchise-practices laws except to the extent of inconsistency. Equal or greater protection is not inconsistent. Completing federal disclosure therefore does not itself establish the state result.

practicalOutput: Check the sale’s actual parties, places and early communications before planning only around the outlet’s state.
limitations: This is a short explanation of relevant facts, not a determination of any state’s reach or exemption.
learningSummary: An opening address alone leaves out facts that state sales laws may treat as relevant. It does not follow that every connection triggers every state’s law.
seoTitle: State franchise sales: buyer, seller and offer locations

title: The deposit can come before the signing deadline
description: Plan the federal waiting period around the earlier relevant commitment, not just final signature.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The general federal period is at least 14 calendar days
paragraphs: For a covered nonexempt franchise to be located in the United States or its territories, the franchisor generally must furnish the current FDD at least 14 calendar days before the prospective franchisee signs a binding agreement with, or pays, the franchisor or an affiliate in connection with the proposed sale.

An affiliate is a related company. Routing a charge to it does not by itself remove the payment question. Calling a payment a reservation or making it refundable does not automatically put it outside the rule either.

sections.heading: A territory deposit changes what must be checked first
paragraphs: A fictional Dutch brand plans final signing near month-end but asks for an earlier deposit to hold the territory. Counting only from final signature misses that earlier event. If the deposit is a relevant payment, the waiting period must be satisfied before it; postponing signature does not cure a premature payment.
The same principle requires examining preliminary agreements and what they actually bind the parties to. This example does not determine the treatment of a particular reservation.

sections.heading: Use the documents actually furnished
paragraphs: Use a permitted delivery method and the rule’s actual counting requirements, including the special treatment of mailing. Keep the current FDD, proposed agreements and exhibits furnished to this recipient and the delivery evidence. A learning-module completion does not establish formal disclosure.
State requirements and later document changes can impose separate questions. A signed receipt is evidence of delivery, not approval of the offering or a waiver of the buyer’s rights.

practicalOutput: Check the earliest relevant agreement or payment before asking the prospect to sign or pay.
limitations: This explains general federal timing; exemptions, delivery/counting facts and independent state or revised-agreement requirements still need application to the transaction.
learningSummary: For a covered nonexempt franchise sale, the FDD must arrive through the required process before the buyer commits. An earlier payment can matter even when the main agreement is signed later.
seoTitle: FDD delivery before franchise payments and agreements

title: Does the new contract term require another waiting period?
description: The origin and material effect of a revision matter; every edit does not restart every clock.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: When the seven-calendar-day rule applies
paragraphs: If the franchisor unilaterally and materially changes the attached basic franchise agreement or related agreements, it must furnish each revised agreement at least seven calendar days before that agreement is signed.

Not every drafting edit is material. Changes arising from negotiations initiated by the prospective franchisee do not trigger this particular period. Calling a brand-proposed change negotiated does not establish that exception.

sections.heading: Two changes in the same transaction
paragraphs: After furnishing the FDD, a fictional brand adds a new field-support charge for all new operators. The prospect did not ask for it. Determine whether that is a unilateral material change requiring the revised delivery and waiting period.

The same prospect asks to move a territory boundary during negotiations. Preserve that different origin rather than classifying both revisions together. A final clean copy alone does not explain who initiated each change or its effect.

sections.heading: This does not replace the general timetable
paragraphs: The general FDD disclosure period and state amendment or further-disclosure requirements are separate. Fix the signing date using the actual revised documents and applicable rules, not a broad assumption that any negotiation either restarts everything or removes all waiting.

practicalOutput: Establish who initiated the change and what it changes before setting the signing date.
limitations: No particular materiality or state-law outcome is decided here. The seven-day trigger concerns signing the revised agreement, not a replacement for every other timing rule.
learningSummary: A brand-initiated new charge and a change requested by the prospect have different histories. The federal revised-agreement rule distinguishes them.
seoTitle: Revised franchise agreements and the seven-day trigger

title: Keep the FDD accurate when the business changes
description: An annual document date does not absorb every later change to support or performance information.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The federal update requirements
paragraphs: Revise the FDD within 120 days after fiscal year-end, then distribute only the revised document. Material changes also require quarterly revisions within a reasonable time after quarter-end; reasonable time is not a fixed invented number of days.

Known material changes in Item 19 financial-performance information must be communicated when the FDD is furnished. Waiting for the next annual revision does not satisfy that separate requirement. State renewals and amendments have their own calendars.

sections.heading: Outsourcing support can change the promise
paragraphs: A fictional French brand moves U.S. field support to a contractor mid-year. Compare the new provider, personnel, commitments and contract wording with what prospects were told. The question is whether required information has materially changed, not whether the brochure still looks current.
Identify who received each version so any needed communication can reach the right prospect. Do not overwrite an earlier furnished document with a later edit under the same filename.

sections.heading: Keep the actual versions and receipts
paragraphs: Materially different FDD versions must be kept for three years after the close of the fiscal year in which each was last used. Signed receipts for completed sales must be kept for at least three years. These are different retention descriptions, not one interchangeable deletion date.

practicalOutput: Compare the changed business promise with the FDD in use and retain the versions actually furnished.
limitations: This does not decide whether a particular event is material or complete a state renewal or amendment requirement.
learningSummary: If the business changes, prospects may need different information from the last annual FDD. Annual updates, quarterly material changes and Item 19 information have different requirements.
seoTitle: FDD annual updates, material changes and retained versions

title: Can you show U.S. prospects your home-market sales figures?
description: A true home-market revenue figure is not automatically a supported U.S. sales claim or evidence of profit.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: A spreadsheet or conversation can carry the claim
paragraphs: The federal definition covers oral, written and visual statements and mathematical calculations about the specified actual or potential sales, income, gross profit or net profit. Calling a figure illustrative does not decide its treatment.

An internal planning model and a recruitment pitch have different audiences. Before using figures with prospects, the representation needs its applicable reasonable basis, written support and disclosure treatment. Brokers and other sellers cannot be left to improvise different claims.

sections.heading: Fictional example: US$1 million in Singapore
paragraphs: A cleaning brand puts a Singapore outlet’s annual revenue, equivalent to US$1 million, beside a U.S. territory map. Correct currency conversion does not establish what a U.S. operator will sell or keep as profit.

The period, customer mix, included and excluded outlets and omitted costs all matter. U.S. management pay, insurance, collections and local sales costs may differ. One strong outlet can also misrepresent the wider group. The meaningful question is what the prospect will infer and whether the evidence supports that message.

sections.heading: Not making a claim still requires an Item 19 answer
paragraphs: A franchisor can elect not to make a financial performance representation, but must give the prescribed negative Item 19 disclosure. That choice does not permit financial-result claims privately or elsewhere in the sales process.

The rule’s specific-outlet-record and compliant supplemental-representation routes have their own conditions. They are not permission to give any figures off-document. Written supporting material alone does not replace the required treatment.

practicalOutput: Compare what the prospect would understand with what the actual data supports before using home-market results in recruitment.
limitations: No source result or projection is approved here. Independent state requirements and the exact conditional disclosure routes remain separate.
learningSummary: Showing existing results can become a regulated financial performance representation. The audience and message matter as well as whether the original accounts are accurate.
seoTitle: Foreign outlet results in U.S. franchise recruitment

title: Will the partner run units or support other business owners?
description: Recruiting independent owners creates work beyond operating your own branches.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The practical difference
paragraphs: An own-unit operator hires staff, wins customers and delivers the service through its business. An area developer typically adds an agreed programme of its own units. A master arrangement can add independent-owner recruitment, disclosure, contracting, training, support and disputes.

An area representative may help recruit or support operators while the brand remains their contracting franchisor. These are practical descriptions, not universal legal definitions; actual rights, payments and conduct matter. Distribution or a brand licence needs its own analysis.

sections.heading: Four managed branches do not prove a franchise-support business
paragraphs: A fictional French maintenance operator successfully runs four branches and proposes recruiting independent U.S. owners. Its record shows employee training and customer delivery, but no franchise-sales process or dedicated owner-support team.

The additional work needs people and recurring funding. If recruitment slows and new upfront territory fees stop, the support obligations do not disappear. Compare that continuing work with the income that will actually fund it.

sections.heading: The intermediary can have its own duties
paragraphs: An intermediary can be a federal subfranchisor when it engages in both pre-sale activities and post-sale performance. Allocating tasks does not erase those duties. Item 21 calls for separate subfranchisor financial statements in the relevant arrangement.
Follow who contracts, receives the fees and performs support. Those relationships may differ; the heading master partner does not decide them.

practicalOutput: Choose the actual own-unit or independent-owner job before granting regional rights, and check how continuing support will be funded.
limitations: No structure, exemption or state-law treatment is selected here. Financial-disclosure requirements depend on the actual arrangement.
learningSummary: A regional title does not describe the job. Decide whether the partner will develop its own units or also sell rights and support independent operators.
seoTitle: Area development versus master-franchise work

title: Why a foreign audit may need more work for the FDD
description: An audit, an acceptable accounting basis and the right reporting companies are three different questions.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Prepared under which rules, and audited under which standards?
paragraphs: Item 21 specifies U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, or principles permitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission, together with applicable U.S. generally accepted auditing standards. The accounting basis governs preparation; audit standards govern the examination. Having an audit does not answer both.

The current Securities and Exchange Commission general filing rule permits foreign private issuers to use International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), or U.S. GAAP. Other comprehensive accounting principles generally require the specified U.S. GAAP reconciliation, subject to the applicable form. SEC staff guidance distinguishes IASB-issued IFRS from home-country standards and requires the stated compliance in the accounts and auditor’s opinion to omit reconciliation. This establishes the general SEC framework; it does not approve this group’s FDD accounts or replace Item 21’s audit requirements.

sections.heading: Parent support can affect the statement question
paragraphs: In a fictional European group, a new U.S. subsidiary will sell franchises while presentations promise parent training and technical support. Budgeting only for the subsidiary’s opening accounts can miss questions raised by the parent’s obligations or guarantees.

Read the actual commitments. A thin seller does not make parent promises disappear, but a strong parent does not automatically let the seller attach the parent’s annual report instead. Subfranchisor roles raise further requirements.

sections.heading: Allow time for the work actually needed
paragraphs: The required companies and reporting periods, preparation basis, audit approach and any reconciliation affect the cost and delivery date of the FDD. Signing an audit engagement is not completion of that work.

The federal startup phase-in is conditional, not a universal shortcut for an established foreign system or any newly formed U.S. seller. State acceptance and financial-assurance conditions are separate.

practicalOutput: Allow for the actual statement and audit work before promising the sales launch date.
limitations: This identifies acceptance issues; it does not determine the exact statements, startup eligibility or state financial conditions for your group.
learningSummary: Existing audited accounts can be useful without automatically satisfying Item 21 of the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD). The U.S. seller, a supporting parent and a subfranchisor can affect which statements are required.
seoTitle: Foreign audits and FDD accounting requirements

title: Is the royalty amount gross or net of withholding?
description: A promised net royalty can cost the payer more than the same amount stated before withholding.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The rate depends on the payment and recipient
paragraphs: Withholding is tax the payer deducts and remits rather than sending it to the foreign recipient. The IRS describes a general 30% regime for many types of U.S.-source income paid to foreign persons. It does not apply at 30% to every cross-border payment: statutory or treaty relief depends on the facts and documentation.

Identify what the payment is for, where the income is sourced and who receives and beneficially owns it—the person entitled to the income for this analysis. A treaty-country address or incorporation certificate does not establish entitlement. Applicable treaty conditions and limitations still matter.

sections.heading: What a gross-up changes
paragraphs: The following figures are fictional cash illustrations using a hypothetical 10% deduction, not a rate for any country. The net-promise row assumes only that deduction, no other adjustment, and rounded amounts.

sections.heading: Budget the receipt, not just the invoice
paragraphs: A gross-up clause may increase the payer’s cost to deliver a specified net amount. In the second illustration, US$100,000 ÷ 0.90 gives the gross payment. The actual contract controls; the arithmetic does not establish a tax rate or treaty benefit.

If support was budgeted to use the whole US$100,000 gross royalty in the first row, the brand has only US$90,000 available before those costs. An unknown applicable rate cannot safely be treated as zero.
The payer also needs to address deductions, deposits, certificates and reporting. Forms 1042 and 1042-S belong to that process; a reduced rate does not itself remove reporting duties.

practicalOutput: Check whether the royalty clause promises a gross payment or a net receipt, then budget the actual withholding and support cash separately.
limitations: No actual rate, treaty entitlement, income-source classification or filing outcome is determined here.
learningSummary: The royalty in the contract may differ from the cash your overseas brand receives. Agree whether the amount is before or after withholding before using it to fund support.
seoTitle: U.S. royalties: withholding, net cash and gross-up

title: Foreign-owned and foreign-formed are different BOI questions
description: Read the company’s formation record before classifying it from the owner’s nationality.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Two Malaysian expansion plans, two entity records
paragraphs: Beneficial ownership information (BOI) is the company ownership information addressed by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) reporting regime discussed here.

In one fictional plan, a Malaysian company creates a new U.S. subsidiary. In another, the Malaysian company itself registers to do business in a state. The subsidiary was created in the United States; the registered parent was formed abroad.
Foreign ownership does not change that formation distinction. The subsidiary’s domestic exemption does not decide a separate registration by its parent, nor every other company in the group.

sections.heading: The foreign-registration branch has its own timing
paragraphs: The final rule effective August 14, 2026 preserves the narrowed scope and specified relief for U.S.-person beneficial-owner and company-applicant information. Older 2024 or early-2025 checklists can describe superseded duties.

For new in-scope reporting companies on or after March 26, 2025, the recorded rule uses 30 calendar days from the earlier actual or public registration notice, subject to applicable relief. Check the actual entity’s exemptions and any judicial or agency relief at the filing date, rather than starting from an internal announcement.

practicalOutput: Use each company’s formation and registration events to establish its BOI position, rather than copying a group-wide answer.
limitations: This is the recorded November 2026 scope, not a new legal update or individual filing decision. IRS reporting, state annual reports, banking and sanctions checks remain separate.
learningSummary: Under the narrowed rule recorded in the November 2026 review, U.S.-created domestic entities are exempt. A nonexempt foreign-formed entity registered by filing in a U.S. state or tribal jurisdiction can remain a reporting company.
seoTitle: FinCEN BOI: U.S.-created versus foreign-formed entities

title: BE-13 can matter before the U.S. business makes a sale
description: A small startup and an exemption claim still need the correct transaction branch.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Buying, establishing and expanding are different
paragraphs: The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) BE-13 survey concerns new foreign direct investment in the United States. Its decision tree separates acquisition, establishment and expansion. Identify the actual event, foreign ownership and voting interests, and relevant costs before choosing a form.
A fictional Singapore services group creates a modest U.S. startup with no premises. It should follow the establishment branch, not assume that the survey concerns only factory acquisitions.

sections.heading: The acquisition threshold is not a startup exemption
paragraphs: The reviewed BE-13A revision 10/2025 uses acquisition cost greater than US$40 million together with a foreign voting-interest condition. That belongs to the acquisition form, not every establishment or expansion.

Below a full-report threshold can still require the prescribed Claim for Exemption. That is a response, not doing nothing. The applicable form’s actual ownership and other conditions must be met; the startup example does not select its response here.

sections.heading: Do not wait for the first invoice
paragraphs: The recorded current decision tree states that forms are due within 45 days of the transaction. Establish the relevant event before the period passes. Later cost updates and other BEA surveys are separate from the initial BE-13 answer.

practicalOutput: Identify the BE-13 branch and relevant event when the investment is made, before assuming no response is needed.
limitations: No actual form selection, exemption or full subsequent BEA-reporting result is determined. The US$40 million condition is limited to the reviewed acquisition form.
learningSummary: Foreign-investment reporting is separate from incorporation and tax. Creating a U.S. company can raise the question before it has customers or premises.
seoTitle: BE-13 reporting for a new foreign-owned U.S. business

title: No revenue does not mean no Form 5472 question
description: Startup funding can matter even while the U.S. LLC is dormant.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The return follows its own scope and transactions
paragraphs: IRS Form 5472 instructions include certain foreign-owned U.S. disregarded entities and describe accompanying pro forma Form 1120 mechanics. The reporting-corporation rules, reportable transactions and exceptions determine the obligation.
Pro forma Form 1120 in this process is not a conclusion that the LLC owes ordinary corporate income tax. Neither one member nor no taxable profit settles the information-return question.

sections.heading: A dormant company can still have transactions
paragraphs: In a fictional example, a foreign parent forms a wholly owned U.S. LLC and sends money for anticipated expenses. There is no customer revenue at year-end. The funding still needs its actual description: a loan, contribution or other arrangement, with the parties and dates established.

Capital contributions, distributions, loans, royalties, intercompany charges and nonmonetary transactions can require examination under the instructions. Listing them does not declare every entry reportable or identically treated.

sections.heading: Use the actual tax year and instructions
paragraphs: Determine the applicable return date and any extension for the actual entity. The instructions describe substantial failure-to-file penalties, but this page does not calculate a universal penalty or assume one was incurred.

practicalOutput: Do not discard the parent-funding question because trading has not started; establish what the transfer actually represents.
limitations: No return obligation or exception is decided here. Entity choice, income tax, treaties, transfer pricing and state rules need their own analysis.
learningSummary: A disregarded income-tax classification does not mean every information return disappears. Certain foreign-owned U.S. entities have special Form 5472 treatment.
seoTitle: Foreign-owned LLC reporting before customer revenue

title: A franchise contract alone does not establish an L-1 company link
description: Brand rights are different from the prescribed ownership and control relationship.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: A strong commercial relationship is not the same corporate relationship
paragraphs: In a fictional case, a German brand licenses an independent U.S. operator and wants its COO to run that business. The brand agreement grants commercial rights; it does not establish the prescribed parent, branch, affiliate or subsidiary link.

The actual ownership, voting and control rights and continuing business matter. The individual’s overseas employment and proposed U.S. duties remain separate requirements; a management title does not supply them. New-office cases require additional evidence.

sections.heading: Do not assume founder relocation is required
paragraphs: An owner may plan partner-operated delivery while staying abroad. If someone will physically work in the United States, identify the actual work, place and duration before the launch depends on it. The staff-transfer guide covers the person and role questions in more detail.

practicalOutput: Check whether the actual company relationship qualifies before making the COO’s U.S. assignment part of the launch promise.
limitations: The regulation was reviewed, but the USCIS policy-manual page was inaccessible; current policy and case-specific treatment remain unverified. No eligibility or alternative route is established.
learningSummary: L-1 concerns a transfer within a qualifying group. A commercial licence to an independently owned operator does not by itself establish that group connection.
seoTitle: L-1 company relationships versus franchise contracts

title: Does a treaty-country subsidiary establish E-2 nationality?
description: Incorporation in a treaty country is not the whole enterprise-nationality inquiry.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Look beyond the intermediate company
paragraphs: A fictional Malaysian-owned group has a Singapore subsidiary and assumes its registration establishes E-2 eligibility. The relevant inquiry needs the ownership chain through to individuals and the actual control rights. Do not fill missing nationality facts from a company’s registered address.

The proposed applicant’s role, investment and control are separate. Principal-investor and employee conditions differ; a budget alone does not establish committed capital at risk or eligibility to develop and direct the enterprise.

sections.heading: Use the actual treaty category and footnotes
paragraphs: The State Department list distinguishes E-1 treaty-trader from E-2 treaty-investor treatment. Appearance in one does not establish the other. Entries can have territorial or historical conditions: the UK footnote, for example, includes nationality and inhabitant conditions.
A passport or a treaty-country company label can therefore leave relevant conditions unanswered. The country list does not replace the ownership, investment and actual-role requirements.

practicalOutput: Trace the actual individual ownership and applicable E-2 entry before treating the subsidiary’s registration as an immigration solution.
limitations: No enterprise or individual eligibility is established. The Foreign Affairs Manual was inaccessible in the recorded review; specific consular and proposed-escrow sufficiency questions remain unresolved.
learningSummary: The regulation traces ownership as practicable to the ultimate individual owners. A subsidiary’s address does not by itself establish that nationality or a person’s E-2 eligibility.
seoTitle: E-2 enterprise nationality and ultimate individual owners

title: Does that court result really belong to your partner?
description: A similar name and a case headline are not enough to attribute a dispute or assess its result.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Match the actual entity
paragraphs: In a fictional search, a bankruptcy result resembles the name of a proposed cleaning partner. Before treating it as adverse information, match the actual legal entity and appropriate public identifiers. If it is another company, the name resemblance is not evidence against the candidate.

PACER’s Case Locator indexes federal appellate, bankruptcy and district cases. It does not cover every state and local court. A blank federal result is not proof of no disputes; former names and other variants can matter too.

sections.heading: Read the record behind the headline
paragraphs: A complaint states allegations. Settlements, consent orders, default judgments and contested judgments have different procedural meanings; read what the actual record resolves. An ordered amount is not proof that money was collected.

Where available, check later relevant orders and procedural status. Leave an uncertain identity or outcome uncertain rather than filling the gap. Court history also does not replace operating evidence, references or evidence of the partner’s accessible project funds.

practicalOutput: Match the company before attributing the case, then use the actual document and its status rather than the search headline.
limitations: This site has investigated or certified no candidate. Federal searches leave state/local courts and broader business diligence separate.
learningSummary: A federal court search can reveal useful evidence. It can also return a different company or miss disputes outside its coverage.
seoTitle: PACER searches: company identity and case outcomes

title: A course badge does not prove FDD delivery
description: A learning tool can explain the offer without satisfying the formal disclosure process.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The document must meet the disclosure rules
paragraphs: An FDD has prescribed content, attachments, format, delivery and retention requirements. The prospect must be able to store, download, print or maintain it. The electronic-format rule permits specified navigation but restricts other multimedia, popups and links to external information.

Putting disclosure paragraphs around an interactive website, calculator or exported planning brief does not automatically create an FDD. A format useful for teaching still needs to meet the actual formal-document rules.

sections.heading: The waiting period does not start with the badge
paragraphs: A fictional brand requires a module about support costs before signing. Its completion can show learning progress, but does not establish formal delivery. Check the required timetable using the actual FDD, agreements and relevant commitment events, not the module’s completion time.

Disclosure and a receipt are not government approval, a profit promise or general permission to sell. Learning progress does not replace the formal delivery evidence. The linked timing guide covers the earlier agreement/payment question.

practicalOutput: Use the formal disclosure document and actual delivery evidence when deciding the signing or payment timetable.
limitations: No website format or delivery method is approved here. Independent state requirements remain separate.
learningSummary: Completing a module does not show that the prospect received the current FDD and proposed agreements. The actual formal document and delivery event matter.
seoTitle: Electronic FDD requirements versus course completion

title: Who gets paid when you sell centrally and the operator delivers?
description: Territory geography does not allocate the customer contract, local costs or collection risk.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Exclusive does not answer every account question
paragraphs: Item 12 requires disclosure of territory terms, exclusivity and conditions, reserved channels and relevant competing operations. The agreement and disclosure should describe the same arrangement. Exclusivity does not protect against unrelated competitors.
Existing reserved accounts, new national buyers, their local branches, online leads and cross-boundary jobs can create different questions within the same map.

sections.heading: A fictional central sale with local delivery
paragraphs: A Dutch maintenance operator asks for five states before completing one pilot. A customer wants one central contract for sites across several areas. Suppose, for this fictional illustration, the brand wins and signs the account and invoices the customer, while a local operator performs one site’s work.

The brand controls collection, but the operator needs staff, equipment, travel and training to deliver. The revenue/cost division is not yet agreed. The map alone does not fund that job. Decide who bids, contracts, delivers, invoices and collects, and how income and costs are allocated—including continuity and compensation if an operator cannot meet the service promise.

sections.heading: A pilot can test capability before a wider commitment
paragraphs: Staged development is an optional commercial choice, not a legal default. Test demand, delivery density and support capacity rather than treating five states as proof of capability. Proposed milestones still need their actual conditions and enforceability examined.

Keep the practical account allocation consistent in negotiation, disclosure and contract. A reservation or milestone does not override non-waivable state protection, and competition questions remain separate.

practicalOutput: Resolve the national account’s local delivery cost and payment terms before committing the operator to serve it.
limitations: The fictional allocation approves no exclusivity, compensation, milestone or account clause. Actual agreements, state relationship protection and competition rules remain separate.
learningSummary: A national customer may buy centrally while receiving service in several territories. Agree what is reserved and who earns and spends the money before promising exclusivity.
